title: Nehemiah 13:15–22
context: Nehemiah sees people in Judah working and trading on the Sabbath and men of Tyre selling in Jerusalem; he rebukes the nobles, reminding them that such profaning brought evil on their fathers and the city. He has the gates shut before the Sabbath and posts guards, warns merchants who camp outside the wall, and commands the Levites to purify themselves and keep the gates. These Sabbath reforms are narrative, and Nehemiah’s prayer for remembrance and mercy (13:22) is shared ground in both traditions.

verses.text: In those days I saw some men treading wine presses on the Sabbath in Judah, bringing in sheaves, and loading donkeys with wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of burdens which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day; and I testified against them in the day in which they sold food.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah sees men “treading wine presses on the Sabbath in Judah, bringing in sheaves, and loading donkeys,” and testifies against them. Arminian readers note that the people had pledged to keep the Sabbath (10:31).

The Sabbath was a gift of rest (Exod 20:8–11).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Sabbath neglected for the sake of commerce.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the narrative records how quickly a covenant pledge can be set aside.

verses.text: Some men of Tyre also lived there, who brought in fish and all kinds of wares, and sold on the Sabbath to the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Some men of Tyre also lived there, who brought in fish and all kinds of wares, and sold on the Sabbath to the children of Judah.” Arminian readers note that the problem involved both buyers and sellers.

The pledge in 10:31 had been not to buy on the Sabbath.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see outside commerce drawing the people from their commitment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the people of Judah were responsible for their own choices.

verses.text: Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said to them, “What evil thing is this that you do, and profane the Sabbath day?
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah contends with the nobles of Judah and asks, “What evil thing is this that you do, and profane the Sabbath day?” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah addresses the leaders first.

Those with influence bear particular responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see leaders called to account.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the reform begins with those who could have prevented the problem.

verses.text: Didn’t your fathers do this, and didn’t our God bring all this evil on us and on this city? Yet you bring more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Didn’t your fathers do this, and didn’t our God bring all this evil on us and on this city?” Arminian readers note the appeal to history, which echoes Jeremiah’s warnings about the Sabbath (Jer 17:21–27).

Past judgment is a warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the exile remembered as judgment for covenant unfaithfulness.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Nehemiah warns that they “bring more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath.”

verses.text: It came to pass that when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors should be shut, and commanded that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. I set some of my servants over the gates, so that no burden should be brought in on the Sabbath day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah commanded “that the doors should be shut, and commanded that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath.” Arminian readers note the practical steps taken to support the reform.

He posts his own servants at the gates.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see wise measures to guard a commitment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: reforms often require practical structures, not only good intentions.

verses.text: So the merchants and sellers of all kinds of wares camped outside of Jerusalem once or twice.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the merchants and sellers of all kinds of wares camped outside of Jerusalem once or twice.” Arminian readers note that the merchants tested the new rule.

The problem did not disappear at once.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see persistence needed in reform.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the narrative honestly reports resistance to change.

verses.text: Then I testified against them, and said to them, “Why do you stay around the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on, they didn’t come on the Sabbath.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah warns them, “If you do so again, I will lay hands on you.” “From that time on, they didn’t come on the Sabbath.” Arminian readers note the firmness of his warning.

The narrative reports its effect.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a governor using his authority to protect the Sabbath.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the account as narrative, not as a model for every setting.

verses.text: I commanded the Levites that they should purify themselves, and that they should come and keep the gates, to sanctify the Sabbath day. Remember me for this also, my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your loving kindness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah commands the Levites to purify themselves and keep the gates, and prays, “Remember me for this also, my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your loving kindness.” Arminian readers note that he appeals to God’s mercy.

The prayer joins faithful work with dependence on grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the appeal resting on God’s loving kindness rather than on Nehemiah’s deeds.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the servant asks to be remembered and spared, trusting God’s character.
